desc:
Given an integer array arr, count the triples (i, j, k) with 0 ≤ i < j ≤ k < n such that a = b, where

  • a = arr[i] XOR arr[i+1] XOR ... XOR arr[j-1]
  • b = arr[j] XOR arr[j+1] XOR ... XOR arr[k]

Both parts are non-empty. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

For example, arr = [2, 3, 1, 6, 7] gives 4, and arr = [1, 1, 1, 1, 1] gives 10.
hints: Three nested loops with a running XOR give O(n3), and it is still O(n2) with prefix XORs. Look for a cleaner condition for a = b.
a = b means a XOR b = 0, and a XOR b is the XOR of the whole range i..k. With prefix XORs P (where P[t] is the XOR of the first t elements) this reads P[i] = P[k+1].

The split point j does not matter for the condition: any of the k - i positions i < j ≤ k works. So every pair of equal prefix values P[i] = P[m] with i < m contributes m - i - 1. Group by prefix value and keep a count and a sum of indices.
editorial: The XOR of the two halves is the XOR of arr[i..k], which equals P[i] XOR P[k+1]. The halves are equal exactly when that is zero, i.e. P[i] = P[k+1], and then the split j can be any of the k - i positions after i up to k.

Write m = k + 1. The answer is the sum over pairs i < m with P[i] = P[m] of m - i - 1. Scanning m from left to right with, for every prefix value v, the number c[v] of earlier indices and their index sum s[v], the contribution of m is c[v] * (m - 1) - s[v]. That makes the whole solution O(n) time and space. The total can reach about C(10,000, 3) = 1.7·1011, hence the modulus.
